module_title: MS Excel - Inbuilt Functions and Cell Referencing Strategies
introduction: This intermediate tier tackles the technical core of Excel: utilizing pre-programmed 'Functions' and understanding how to 'lock' cells using Cell Referencing, which is heavily tested in practical and statement-based questions.

core_concepts.title: Formula vs. Function
core_concepts.description:
- Formula: A custom mathematical equation manually typed by the user (e.g., `=A1+B1+C1`).
- Function: A pre-programmed, inbuilt formula provided by Excel to make complex calculations instantly (e.g., `=SUM(A1:C1)`).

core_concepts.title: Crucial Basic Functions
core_concepts.description:
- `=SUM(A1:A5)`: Adds all numbers in the specified range.
- `=AVERAGE(A1:A5)`: Calculates the mean average.
- `=COUNT(A1:A5)`: Counts strictly only the cells that contain NUMBERS.
- `=MAX(A1:A5)` & `=MIN(A1:A5)`: Finds the highest and lowest values in a range.

core_concepts.title: Cell Referencing (The Power of $)
core_concepts.description:
When you drag/copy a formula down a column, Excel automatically shifts the cell addresses. To stop this, we 'lock' the cells using the Dollar sign (`$`). There are 3 types:
1. Relative Reference (e.g., `A1`): The default state. Addresses change automatically when copied.
2. Absolute Reference (e.g., `$A$1`): Both the column (A) and row (1) are fully locked. The address will never change when copied.
3. Mixed Reference (e.g., `$A1` or `A$1`): Only one element (either the row or the column) is locked.

important_entities.name: The Colon ( : )
important_entities.significance: A colon placed between two cell addresses defines a continuous 'Range'. For example, `A1:A10` means 'every cell starting from A1 down to A10'.

important_entities.name: The F4 Key
important_entities.significance: While typing a formula, highlighting a cell reference and pressing the `F4` key instantly applies the dollar signs to make it an Absolute Reference (locks it).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Aspirants assume `=COUNT()` counts everything. False! It strictly counts cells containing numbers. If you want to count cells containing ANYTHING (text, symbols, numbers), you must use the `=COUNTA()` (Count All) function. This is a massive trap.
When calculating an average, the `=AVERAGE()` function completely ignores blank/empty cells. However, if a cell contains a literal '0', it WILL be counted and will drastically lower the average.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Whatever character is directly 'behind' the dollar sign is locked in place. In `$A1`, only Column A is locked. Row 1 can still change.

exam_strategy_tips: SSC CGL Tier-1 frequently asks: 'Which symbol is used to create an Absolute Cell Reference in MS Excel?' The answer is always the Dollar symbol ($).
